evidence: Plin. NH 15.85: aliīs ōvāta speciēs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Pliny’s word, from ōvum, egg; Lewis & Short marks it post-Augustan. For the shape as a noun, fōrma ōvāta or simply ōvātum; a modern Latin description gives it as “round out of long”, ex longō rotunda (M-O s.v. oval, from Egger).

evidence: M-O s.v. ellipse; oval (subst.), from Egger
terms.comment: The modern geometer’s word. Classically ellipsis is only the figure of speech (an omission).

evidence: Gell. 5.6.20: ovālis corōna murtea est (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A false friend: classically the myrtle crown of an ovātiō, the lesser triumph, from ovō with a short o, not from ōvum. Renaissance writers make a new word of it for “oval” (Mercuriale’s ovalem, M-O s.v. triangle: rectangular); ōvātus says it without the clash.

phrases.latin: Hoc nōn rotundum est, sed ōvātum, ut ōvum.
phrases.english: This isn’t round, it’s oval, like an egg.

phrases.latin: Ōvum pinge: nōn rotundum, sed paulō longius.
phrases.english: Draw an egg: not round, but a bit longer.

phrases.latin: terra māter est in mediō quasi ōvum corrotundāta, et omnia bona in sē habet tanquam favus
phrases.english: mother earth is in the middle, rounded like an egg, and holds every good thing in her like a honeycomb

sources: Lewis & Short: ovatus · Lewis & Short: ovalis · Lewis & Short: ellipsis
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. oval; ellipse; triangle: rectangular.
